\chapter{Lo Que Llevas --- Clock, Phone, Suitcase, Map, Letter}
\label{ch:lo-que-llevas}
\hlchaptermodality{312}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name and ask for the five things I travel with in Spanish: the clock, the phone, the suitcase, the map and the letter.}

Complete ES-C312-carta: ask for each of the five carried things, and ask for the menu by the same word.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el reloj]{el reloj — the hour-teller, squeezed down to two syllables}

\label{lesson:ES-C312-reloj}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time. What is \emph{la bolsa}? (The bag.) And what does an assessor do, going by the root? (Sits beside.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{re-LOJ}, stress on the end. The initial \emph{r} is rolled, and the final \emph{j} is that scraped sound at the back of the throat. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el reloj} — \textquotedblleft{}the clock,\textquotedblright{} and also the watch on your wrist.

Behind it is \textbf{horologium}, which Latin had from Greek: \emph{hōra}, the \textbf{hour}, plus a stem meaning \textbf{to tell}. A clock is an \textbf{hour-teller}. That is the entire description, and it is still accurate.

Spanish reached \emph{reloj} by way of Catalan \emph{relotge}, and you can watch the word lose weight at every step. \emph{Horologium} has five syllables. \emph{Relotge} has three. \emph{Reloj} has two. The \emph{h-} went, the \emph{-ium} went, the middle collapsed. What is left is barely recognisable — until you know what to look for.

The \emph{hōra} half is easy to find in English. An \textbf{hour} is one. \textbf{Horology} is the study of timekeeping, and a \textbf{horologist} repairs watches. A \textbf{horoscope} is an \emph{hour-watcher}: the reading of which sky stood over the hour you were born.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of the things already in your pocket rather than behind a counter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el reloj}
  \item \emph{el reloj, por favor}
  \item \emph{disculpe, ¿dónde está el reloj?}
  \item \emph{la bolsa}, then \emph{el asiento}, then \emph{el reloj}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{horologium} mean, taken apart? (Hour-teller.) What is a horoscope watching? (The hour.) And what is \emph{el asiento}? (The seat.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el teléfono]{el teléfono — a far-voice, and where both halves went}

\label{lesson:ES-C312-telefono}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time. What is \emph{el asiento}? (The seat.) And what does a \emph{reloj} tell, going by its root? (The hour.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{te-LÉ-fo-no}. The written accent is doing real work: it tells you the stress lands three syllables from the end, which Spanish always marks. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el teléfono} — \textquotedblleft{}the telephone.\textquotedblright{}

Two Greek pieces, and neither is old in this combination. \textbf{Tele} means \textbf{far}. \textbf{Phone} means \textbf{voice} or \textbf{sound}. A telephone is a \textbf{far-voice}, and the word was built in the nineteenth century by people who needed a name for a thing that had never existed.

That is what makes it useful: both halves are still productive, so knowing them unlocks a shelf of words rather than one.

\emph{Tele-} puts distance in front of anything. A \textbf{telescope} looks far. A \textbf{telegram} writes far. \textbf{Television} sees far. \textbf{Telepathy} feels far.

\emph{-Phone} puts sound at the end. \textbf{Phonetics} is the study of speech sounds. A \textbf{megaphone} is a big sound. A \textbf{microphone} is a small one made large. A \textbf{symphony} is sounds \emph{together}. \textbf{Cacophony} is sounds gone wrong.

Spanish and English built this word out of the same two bricks at almost the same moment, which is why it needs no translation at all.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two pocket objects, and a pair of Greek pieces that will keep paying.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el teléfono}
  \item \emph{el teléfono, por favor}
  \item \emph{disculpe — el teléfono, por favor}
  \item \emph{el asiento}, then \emph{el reloj}, then \emph{el teléfono}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do \emph{tele} and \emph{phone} each mean? (Far, and voice.) What is a symphony, taken apart? (Sounds together.) And what is \emph{el reloj}? (The clock.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la maleta]{la maleta — the bag that gave its name to the post}

\label{lesson:ES-C312-maleta}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time. What is \emph{el reloj}? (The clock.) And what does \emph{tele-} mean in front of a word? (Far.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ma-LE-ta}, stress on the middle. The single \emph{l} is clear and light, made at the front of the mouth. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la maleta} — \textquotedblleft{}the suitcase.\textquotedblright{}

The \emph{-eta} on the end is a diminutive: a \emph{maleta} is a \textbf{little mala}. So what was a \emph{mala}?

Not a Latin word at all. \textbf{Mala} was Gaulish — the language spoken across France before Latin arrived — and it meant a bag or a sack. Latin borrowed it from the people it had conquered, French kept it as \emph{male}, and Spanish took the small version.

Now follow the same bag into English. A rider carrying letters between towns carried them in a \emph{male} — a leather sack strapped behind the saddle. The sack was the visible thing, so people named the service after it. The letters became \textbf{the mail}.

English \emph{mail}, then, is not about letters and never was. It is a bag. Your suitcase and your inbox are the same Gaulish sack, and one of them still admits it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three things you carry, and one of them just explained a word you use every day in English.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la maleta}
  \item \emph{la maleta, por favor}
  \item \emph{disculpe — la maleta, por favor}
  \item \emph{el reloj}, then \emph{el teléfono}, then \emph{la maleta}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was a \emph{mala}? (A Gaulish bag.) Why is the post called \emph{mail}? (Because the letters rode in that bag.) And what is \emph{el teléfono}, taken apart? (A far-voice.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el mapa]{el mapa — the world, drawn on a napkin}

\label{lesson:ES-C312-mapa}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time. What is a \emph{teléfono}, in its two Greek pieces? (A far-voice.) And why is the post called \emph{mail}? (It is named after the bag.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{MA-pa}, stress on the first part. It ends in \emph{-a} and takes \emph{el}, which is worth noticing rather than fighting. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el mapa} — \textquotedblleft{}the map.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{mappa} meant a \textbf{cloth} — a napkin, a signalling flag, a sheet of fabric. The Romans had probably taken the word from Punic, the language of Carthage.

A medieval world map was called a \emph{mappa mundi}: the \textbf{cloth of the world}. Not because the drawing was clever but because the surface was linen. Paper was scarce and small; cloth came in sheets big enough to hold an ocean. English then kept only the first half of the phrase, and \emph{mappa} alone came to mean the drawing rather than the fabric.

The other half of \emph{mappa} went into the kitchen. French turned it into \emph{nappe}, a tablecloth, with the \emph{m} worn down to \emph{n} — and English borrowed the little version as \textbf{napkin}. It even got a second one by accident: \emph{a napron} was misheard as \emph{an apron}, and English has said \emph{apron} ever since.

A map, a napkin and an apron. One Latin cloth, three jobs.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four carried things, and two of them turned out to be bags and cloths rather than the objects you thought.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el mapa}
  \item \emph{el mapa, por favor}
  \item \emph{disculpe — el mapa, por favor}
  \item \emph{el teléfono}, then \emph{la maleta}, then \emph{el mapa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{mappa} mean? (A cloth.) Which two kitchen words come off it? (\emph{Napkin} and \emph{apron}.) And what is \emph{la maleta}? (The suitcase.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la carta]{la carta — one sheet of papyrus, six English words}

\label{lesson:ES-C312-carta}



\begin{quote}
Two from last time. What is \emph{la maleta}? (The suitcase.) And what was a \emph{mappa}? (A cloth.)
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{CAR-ta}, stress on the first part. The \emph{r} is a single tap of the tongue, not a roll. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la carta} — \textquotedblleft{}the letter,\textquotedblright{} and on a table, \textquotedblleft{}the menu.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{charta} came from Greek \emph{khartēs}: a \textbf{sheet of papyrus}. The word named the material, and everything since has been named after the material.

English has the sheet six ways over. A \textbf{chart} is a sheet with information on it. A \textbf{charter} is a sheet with rights on it, which is why a town could be granted one. \textbf{Cartography} is sheet-drawing. A \textbf{carton} is a stiffened sheet folded into a box. A \textbf{cartoon} was originally the full-size drawing on a sheet that a painter worked out before touching the wall. And a \textbf{card} is a small stiff one.

You have met this sheet's cousin already. \emph{El papel} is named after the papyrus plant; \emph{la carta} is named after the sheet cut from it. The plant and the sheet became two different words, and Spanish uses both.

On a menu the logic is unchanged. \emph{La carta} is the sheet the dishes are written on, and \emph{a la carta} means chosen off that sheet.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five things you carry: the clock, the phone, the suitcase, the map, the letter. Four of the five turned out to be named after the stuff they were made of rather than the job they do.

Next comes the counter, where you hand these over.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la carta}
  \item \emph{la carta, por favor}
  \item \emph{disculpe — la carta, por favor}
  \item \emph{la maleta}, then \emph{el mapa}, then \emph{la carta}
  \item \emph{gracias}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was a \emph{khartēs}? (A sheet of papyrus.) What was a \emph{cartoon} before it was funny? (A full-size drawing on a sheet.) And what is \emph{el mapa}? (The map.)
\end{tcolorbox}
